items.followUp: Define a host and give two examples of parasites.

rubric.why: A parasite lives on or inside another organism and obtains nourishment from it.
rubric.description: Defines a parasite by its relationship with a host.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it lives on or in a host and obtains food or nutrients from the host.

rubric.why: Examples show that the student can identify parasites.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two correct examples.

modelAnswer: A parasite is an organism that lives on or inside another organism, called its host, and obtains food from it.
Some parasites, such as tapeworms, harm their hosts.

items.followUp: Name the scientist who proposed the three-kingdom classification and list its kingdoms.

rubric.why: The defining feature of this classification is grouping organisms into three kingdoms.
rubric.description: States that organisms are classified into three kingdoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it divides organisms into three kingdoms.

rubric.why: These are the three kingdoms in the system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming all three kingdoms.

modelAnswer: Three-kingdom classification is a system that groups organisms into three kingdoms.
The kingdoms are Protista, Plantae and Animalia.

items.followUp: State two human activities that can lead to the extinction of species.

rubric.why: These activities can directly reduce populations or destroy the places species need to survive.
rubric.description: Identifies a cause such as habitat loss or overexploitation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid cause of extinction.

rubric.why: These pressures can further threaten populations and cause species to disappear.
rubric.description: Identifies a second cause of extinction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another valid cause.

modelAnswer: Major causes of species extinction include habitat destruction and overexploitation, such as overhunting.
Pollution, climate change and the introduction of invasive species can also cause extinction.

items.followUp: State one structural feature of centrioles and one function of the centrosome.

rubric.why: A centriole is a cylindrical structure composed of microtubules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying its cylindrical form or microtubule structure.

rubric.why: The centrosome contains a pair of centrioles and helps organize spindle fibres during cell division.
rubric.description: Distinguishes the centrosome from a centriole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the centrosome contains two centrioles or organizes spindle fibres.

modelAnswer: A centriole is a cylindrical structure made of microtubules.
A centrosome is the cell region containing a pair of centrioles; it helps organize spindle fibres during cell division.

items.followUp: Where are ribosomes found, and what do they do?

rubric.why: Ribosomes occur freely in the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum.
Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying protein synthesis as their function.

modelAnswer: Ribosomes are found freely in the cytoplasm and attached to the endoplasmic reticulum.
They are the sites of protein synthesis.

items.followUp: What happens to a cell when it enters the G₀ phase?

rubric.why: Cells enter G₀ by leaving the active cell cycle, usually from G₁.
rubric.description: States how a cell enters G₀.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the cell exits the cell cycle or leaves G₁.

rubric.why: A cell in G₀ is not actively dividing, although it may continue normal metabolic functions.
rubric.description: Describes the cell's state in G₀.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it does not divide; credit continued metabolic activity if included.

modelAnswer: In G₀, a cell leaves the active cell cycle, usually from G₁.
It does not divide, but it may remain metabolically active and carry out its normal functions.

items.followUp: How does cytokinesis occur in plant cells?

rubric.why: In animal cells, the cell membrane constricts to form a cleavage furrow.
rubric.description: Identifies the mechanism of cytokinesis in animal cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the formation of a cleavage furrow or constriction of the membrane.

rubric.why: The furrow deepens inward and separates the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.
rubric.description: Describes the direction or outcome of the furrow's action.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the constriction proceeds inward and divides the cell.

modelAnswer: In animal cells, the plasma membrane constricts at the cell's equator to form a cleavage furrow.
The furrow deepens from the outside inward and separates the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.

items.followUp: What happens to enzyme activity above an enzyme's optimum temperature, and why?

rubric.why: Warming increases molecular movement and enzyme-substrate collisions, so activity rises up to the optimum temperature.
rubric.description: Describes the rise in activity as temperature increases to the optimum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that activity increases up to an optimum, or explaining the increased collisions.

rubric.why: Above the optimum, heat alters the enzyme's shape and active site, reducing its activity.
rubric.description: Describes the effect of temperatures above the optimum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the enzyme denatures or its activity decreases above the optimum.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, enzyme activity increases up to an optimum because molecules move faster and enzyme-substrate collisions become more frequent.
Above the optimum temperature, the enzyme denatures and its active site changes shape, so its activity decreases.
